forces.title: High input costs and extreme weather pressure food and beverage margins
forces.description: Food and beverage producers, including those in meat, poultry, and seafood, continue to face significant margin pressure from elevated input costs. High energy and staffing costs, coupled with global market disruptions and extreme weather conditions (like Western Europe's high temperatures and low rainfall in summer 2026), are adversely affecting agricultural yields and production costs. These factors lead to increased cost of raw materials and operational expenses, impacting profitability across the sector.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Food and Drink Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook August 2026

forces.title: Mackerel fishing quota reductions impact Irish seafood sector
forces.description: Ireland's mackerel fishing quota was revised from a proposed -70% to -48% in March 2026, adding approximately 8,000 tonnes to the annual national quota. Despite this revision, the reduction remains substantial and poses a significant challenge for Irish fishers and the seafood processing sector. Although higher mackerel pricing (€5.85 per kg, +165%) is helping to offset some of the volume impact, the overall reduction in available catch represents a notable headwind for seafood producers and exporters.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Food and Drink Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook August 2026

forces.title: EU Deforestation Regulation increases supply chain traceability for commodities
forces.description: From December 2026, the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) will require companies placing commodities like cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soy, and wood on the EU market to demonstrate that their products are deforestation-free and legally produced. This regulation significantly increases supply chain traceability and compliance requirements for Irish food producers involved with these commodities, particularly impacting meat (cattle) and potentially feed inputs derived from soy or palm oil.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Food and Drink Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook August 2026

forces.title: M&A activity continues to expand product ranges and operational scale
forces.description: M&A activity in the food and beverage sector continued in 2026, demonstrating ongoing investment and strategic expansion. An example is the acquisition of Glenhaven Foods, a Co Wicklow-based poultry operator, by Swedish poultry giant Scandi Standard for €127 million. This deal is set to expand Scandi Standard's Ready-to-Eat and value-added range, indicating a trend towards consolidation and product portfolio diversification within the poultry sub-segment to enhance market presence and efficiency.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Food and Drink Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook August 2026

forces.title: Rising fuel, processing, and transport costs tighten agrifood margins
forces.description: Ireland's agrifood sector, including meat, poultry, and seafood producers, faces profitability tightening due to persistent cost pressures. Rising fuel prices, increased processing, and transport costs, exacerbated by the Middle East conflict, are weighing heavily on margins. Businesses, especially smaller producers and hospitality-linked operators, need to manage these costs carefully through cash-flow forecasting, reviewing supplier terms, and monitoring customer payment behaviour to mitigate insolvency pressure.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Increasing input prices for fertiliser, feed, and fuel impact agriculture
forces.description: Irish agriculture is experiencing increasing prices for key inputs such as fertiliser, feed, and fuel in 2026. Fertiliser prices began moving upwards in Q2 2026, while energy prices, particularly agri-diesel, also rose due to the US/Israel war with Iran. These increases directly raise production costs for meat, poultry, and dairy farmers, affecting their profitability. Although feed prices have been relatively stable, the overall upward trend in major inputs poses a significant challenge.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Unfavourable weather conditions affect grass growth and crop yields
forces.description: Irish agriculture is grappling with challenging weather conditions in H1 2026, characterized by unusually high rainfall in autumn/winter 2025/2026 and moderate spring grass growth, followed by a period of high temperatures and lack of rainfall in mid-July. This volatility has negatively impacted grass production for livestock (dairy, beef, sheep) and cereal crop yields for feed. These conditions directly influence input availability and costs for meat and dairy producers.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Lower international butter and cheddar prices reduce Irish milk prices
forces.description: The Irish milk price is primarily weakened by a sharp dip in international butter prices, which remained weaker in 2026, alongside declining cheddar prices. European butter prices stood at close to €3,900 per tonne, and cheddar prices just above €3,140 by the end of H2 2026. This commodity price weakness directly reduces the farmgate milk price, contributing to a significant decline in dairy farm margins despite some stability in SMP prices.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Resilient global dairy demand and slowing supply may improve prices
forces.description: International dairy product demand was robust in Q1 2026, supported by lower prices that stimulated frontloading of purchases, especially in South-East Asia and the Middle East. Despite a cautious global economic outlook, dairy demand is expected to remain relatively resilient. Furthermore, global milk supply growth is slowing, which should lead to some dairy commodity price improvements later in H2 2026, offering a potential uplift to currently depressed milk prices for Irish dairy farmers.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Contracting EU beef supply and stable UK production impacts market dynamics
forces.description: EU beef supply decreased by 1.5% in Q1 2026 and is expected to decline by 2.6% for the full year compared to 2025. This contraction in supply, coupled with a slight decrease in EU beef exports and an expected increase in EU imports, indicates a shifting market dynamic. While the UK's beef production is anticipated to remain similar to 2025 levels, the overall reduction in EU supply affects availability and potentially pricing power within the European beef market.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: EU ewe flock contraction and reduced slaughter lowers sheep meat production
forces.description: The EU ewe flock continues to contract, leading to a decrease in sheep slaughter numbers. Consequently, EU sheep meat production in 2026 is expected to be at least 3% lower than in 2025. This reduction in supply is a significant headwind for the sheep meat market, affecting overall availability. Although higher EU prices are attracting increased imports from the UK and New Zealand, the underlying contraction in domestic production remains a challenge.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Lower lamb supply and higher world prices support Irish lamb market
forces.description: Irish lamb prices are expected to be supported through the remainder of 2026 due to a lower supply of lambs across Irish, EU, and UK markets, combined with higher world prices. Although average Irish lamb prices for the year to date were 2% lower than in 2025, recent increases are anticipated to be maintained, forecasting annual average prices to be circa 3% higher than in 2025. This demand-supply imbalance provides a tailwind for sheep farmers.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Rising farm gate prices for beef, dairy, and poultry affect grocery inflation
forces.description: Irish grocery inflation remains elevated at approximately 4% in June/July 2026, partly driven by rising farm gate prices across beef, dairy, and poultry. These increases contribute to the overall food price inflation faced by consumers and retailers. While higher farm gate prices might offer some relief to producers, they simultaneously exert pressure on consumer purchasing power and require retailers to balance value offerings against cost increases, highlighting the interconnectedness of the supply chain.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Retail Convenience H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

forces.title: Middle East conflict drives inflationary pressure and supply chain risks for agriculture
forces.description: The Middle East conflict presents a material inflationary risk for agriculture, with oil prices reaching over $125/barrel, directly impacting input costs like fertiliser, feed, and fuel. This leads to margin compression and increased volatility for farm systems. While Ireland is less exposed in the short term, prolonged conflict threatens global food security due to potential fertiliser shortages and soaring agricultural costs. Future impacts may include shifts in planting decisions and complex price movements for grain, dairy, and meat.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Prolonged conflict may increase long-term prices for meat and dairy
forces.description: A persistent Middle East conflict, by impacting global energy and fertilizer supplies, could lead to a reduction in grain supply and an increase in feed prices in the longer term. This scenario, while raising feed costs, is also projected to have a positive net effect on farm grain prices and, consequently, a positive impact on meat and dairy prices as global production becomes more expensive. This structural shift could benefit producers in these sectors over time by pushing up output prices.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Fish quota reductions and tariffs pressure seafood and alcoholic beverages
forces.description: The seafood sub-sector in Ireland faces additional pressures in 2026 due to fishing quota reductions. These reductions, alongside tariffs and weakened consumer spending, specifically impact the profitability and export potential for seafood producers. While some quota revisions provide relief, the overall environment for fisheries and marine products remains challenging, necessitating operational adjustments and strategic adaptations to manage reduced catch volumes and market access issues.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Investment in hen housing and animal welfare drives poultry sector growth
forces.description: The poultry sub-sector is seeing continued capital expenditure in hen housing infrastructure. This investment is driven by the need to comply with enhanced animal welfare standards and to support growing consumer demand for eggs. Such strategic capital deployment not only ensures regulatory adherence but also positions producers to capitalize on increasing market demand, signifying a positive long-term growth driver for the poultry industry within the food and beverage sector.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Growing regulatory and administrative demands may drive sector consolidation
forces.description: The increasing regulatory and administrative demands faced by food and beverage producers in Ireland may drive selective consolidation across the sector. Smaller firms might seek scale through mergers or strategic partnerships to better manage compliance requirements, operational efficiencies, and cost pressures. This trend indicates a structural shift where economies of scale and robust governance frameworks become critical for sustained competitiveness and market presence in a demanding operating environment.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Increased supply variability and logistical bottlenecks challenge commodity trading
forces.description: Agricultural commodity markets face increased supply variability and logistical bottlenecks, making it harder for traders and processors to anticipate shifts. Factors include more frequent and intense weather outliers, vacillating trade policies, and price volatility. This environment complicates the management of inputs for meat, poultry, and seafood producers, as unpredictability in commodity availability and pricing creates operational complexity and margin pressure across the value chain, from growers to end markets.
forces.source_title: How agility and AI could rewire agriculture trading

forces.title: Inflation, fertilizer, and fuel availability increase working capital requirements
forces.description: Heightened uncertainty surrounding inflation and the physical availability of fertiliser and fuel introduces new challenges for growers, trading houses, and processors within the agricultural sector. The combination of increased market volatility and ongoing changes in interest rates has amplified pressure from additional working-capital requirements. Market players face elevated capital costs for carrying inventories and increased collateral needed to meet margin obligations at major commodities exchanges, affecting cash flow and investment capacity for meat, poultry, and seafood producers.
forces.source_title: How agility and AI could rewire agriculture trading

forces.title: New market entrants and algorithmic trading intensify agricultural commodity markets
forces.description: The agricultural commodity trading space is becoming more complex with new entrants such as hedge funds, oil and gas incumbents, and even FMCG and food service companies actively participating. These new players, leveraging sophisticated analytics and algorithms, are speeding up price discovery and eroding historical information asymmetry. FMCG and food service companies, in particular, are dynamically hedging for value, which can intensify competition and create trading profitability headwinds for traditional players in the supply chain feeding into meat, poultry, and seafood.
forces.source_title: How agility and AI could rewire agriculture trading

viewpoints.title: Irish Food & Beverage exports decline, producers face margin pressure and competition
viewpoints.description: The Irish food and beverage sector saw exports decline by 3% in H1 2026, with meat, seafood, dairy, and beverages all contracting. Producers continue to face significant margin pressure from high energy, staffing costs, global market disruption, and extreme weather affecting yields. Softening international demand and heightened competition create a challenging environment for exporters. Despite demonstrated resilience, operators maintain a cautious approach to investment, prioritizing efficiency.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Food and Drink Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook August 2026

viewpoints.title: Irish dairy farm margins to sharply reduce by almost 50% in 2026
viewpoints.description: Irish dairy farms are forecast to experience a significant reduction in net margin in 2026, estimated at almost 50% compared to 2025 levels. This sharp decline is attributed to higher milk production costs, which are projected to be around 37 cents per litre (up 5% from 2025), and significantly lower milk prices. While dairy farmers benefit from elevated beef prices through calf and cull cow sales, this only partially offsets the primary pressures.
viewpoints.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

viewpoints.title: Irish sheep farm incomes set to decrease despite modest gross margin gains
viewpoints.description: Average Irish sheep farm income for 2026 is forecast to be lower than 2025 levels, estimated at circa €26,000. While gross margins from sheep production are expected to increase modestly by about 2% to €906 per hectare, this gain will be more than offset by forecast reductions in cattle margins from subsidiary livestock enterprises on these farms. Rising input costs, particularly for fertiliser (up 20%) and fuel, contribute to an overall increase in production costs.
viewpoints.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

viewpoints.title: Agrifood sector stable but profitability tightening due to rising costs
viewpoints.description: Ireland's agrifood sector in Q2 2026 remains relatively resilient, but profitability is anticipated to tighten. This pressure stems from rising fuel prices and increased processing and transport costs, which are directly linked to the Middle East conflict. The overall stability of the sector near-term is highly dependent on the evolution of these cost conditions, broader demand trends, and the macroeconomic environment. Smaller producers and processors are advised to focus on cash-flow forecasting and supplier terms.

viewpoints.title: Greek Food and Beverage industry shows strong growth prospects despite challenges
viewpoints.description: The Greek Food and Beverage industry is a resilient and important pillar of the economy, contributing substantially to GDP and exports. It maintains strong growth prospects due to the high quality of its products, export momentum, and a consumer shift towards healthier foods. However, the sector faces significant challenges including increased energy costs, international inflationary pressures, competition from foreign markets, and the need for sustainable production and digital transformation.
viewpoints.source_title: Food and Beverages Industry. Facts & Figures 2025

viewpoints.title: Irish agriculture outlook challenging with rising input costs and weaker output prices
viewpoints.description: The outlook for Irish agriculture in 2026 is significantly more challenging than initially expected, with average farm incomes projected to reduce. Adverse weather conditions, increasing input costs, and weakening output prices are expected to squeeze farm profitability. The Middle East conflict exacerbates this, directly impacting energy and fertiliser prices, which constitute a large share of production costs. While the FAO Food Price Index rose, positive price developments for key agri commodities like meat and dairy have been limited so far.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: Irish food and beverage faces rising costs, regulation, and sub-sector specific pressures
viewpoints.description: The Irish food and beverage sector, despite strong 2025 export value, faces a challenging environment in 2026. High input costs persist, and the Middle East conflict impacts supply chains and energy. Specifically, seafood and alcoholic beverages are under pressure from fish quota reductions and weakened consumer spend. Regulatory demands like new EU packaging and waste rules also add complexity. The focus for 2026 is operational resilience, automation, efficiency, and compliance rather than expansion.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: Agricultural commodity trading profit pool declined 15% amid increasing volatility
viewpoints.description: The profit pool for agricultural commodity trading declined by 15% year-over-year in 2025, reaching a four-year low since 2022. This decline is attributed to the increased frequency and intensity of weather outliers, fluctuating trade policies, new biofuel regulations, price volatility, and logistical bottlenecks, making it challenging to anticipate shifts in supply, demand, and trade flows. Beef, a long-cycle commodity, experienced tightened supplies due to breeding herd contractions, leading to price increases, but growers overall are struggling with elevated input costs.
viewpoints.source_title: How agility and AI could rewire agriculture trading
